questions.question: What is MapReduce?

options.text: A distributed file system for storing large datasets
A programming model for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster
A NoSQL database for key-value storage
A data compression algorithm for big data

questions.explanation: MapReduce: programming model from Google (2004). Two phases: Map (transform/filter data in parallel), Reduce (aggregate results). Enables processing petabytes across thousands of machines. Foundation of big data.

questions.question: What happens in the Map phase?

options.text: Input is split and processed in parallel, emitting key-value pairs

questions.explanation: Map phase: input split into chunks, each processed by a mapper in parallel. Mapper reads records, applies function, emits (key, value) pairs. Example: word count mapper emits (word, 1) for each word.

questions.question: What happens in the Reduce phase?

options.text: Values with the same key are grouped and aggregated together

questions.explanation: Reduce phase: shuffle groups all values by key, reducer processes each group. Example: word count reducer receives ('hello', [1,1,1]), outputs ('hello', 3). Aggregation, summarization, joining.

questions.question: What is the shuffle phase in MapReduce?

options.text: Transferring map outputs to reducers, grouping by key

questions.explanation: Shuffle: between map and reduce. Sorts map outputs by key, transfers to appropriate reducers (partitioned by key). Most expensive phase—involves network transfer and disk I/O. Optimization target.

questions.question: What is a combiner in MapReduce?

options.text: A component that merges multiple input files before processing
A local reducer that runs on map output before shuffle, reducing data transfer
A data splitter that partitions input across mappers
A network device that routes data between nodes

questions.explanation: Combiner: mini-reducer on mapper node. Aggregates locally before shuffle. Word count: instead of sending (word,1) 1000 times, combiner sends (word,1000). Reduces network traffic. Must be associative/commutative.

questions.question: What is Apache Hadoop?

options.text: An open-source framework implementing MapReduce with HDFS for distributed storage

questions.explanation: Hadoop: open-source implementation of Google's MapReduce and GFS papers. Components: HDFS (storage), MapReduce/YARN (processing). Ecosystem: Hive, Pig, HBase, Spark. Revolutionized big data processing.

questions.question: What is a limitation of MapReduce?

options.text: High latency due to disk I/O between stages; not suitable for iterative algorithms or real-time

questions.explanation: MapReduce limitations: writes to disk between stages (slow), batch-only (no streaming), poor for iterative algorithms (ML), complex multi-stage jobs. Led to Spark (in-memory), Flink (streaming).

questions.question: How does MapReduce achieve fault tolerance?

options.text: Re-executes failed tasks; intermediate data written to disk enables recovery

questions.explanation: MapReduce fault tolerance: if mapper fails, re-run on another node (input from HDFS). If reducer fails, re-run (map outputs on disk). Master tracks progress, reschedules failed tasks. Handles commodity hardware failures.

questions.question: What is data locality in MapReduce?

options.text: Scheduling map tasks on nodes that have the input data to minimize network transfer

questions.explanation: Data locality: move compute to data. HDFS stores blocks on multiple nodes. MapReduce scheduler prefers nodes with local data. Avoids transferring terabytes over network. Key optimization.

questions.question: What replaced MapReduce for many use cases?

options.text: Apache Spark—in-memory processing, faster for iterative algorithms and interactive queries

questions.explanation: Spark largely replaced MapReduce: in-memory processing (10-100x faster), better for ML (iterative), interactive queries, streaming. Same fault tolerance, better performance. MapReduce still used for some batch jobs.

questions.question: Write a word count MapReduce job conceptually. What do map and reduce functions do?

options.text: Map: emit (word, 1) for each word; Reduce: sum all 1s for each word
Map: sort words; Reduce: delete duplicates

questions.explanation: Word count: Map(line) → for each word emit (word, 1). Shuffle groups by word. Reduce(word, [1,1,1,...]) → emit (word, sum). Classic MapReduce example. Parallelizes across documents, aggregates counts.

questions.question: A company needs to process 100TB of log files to count error types. Best approach?

options.text: MapReduce or Spark job: map extracts error types, reduce counts each type

questions.explanation: 100TB log analysis: perfect for MapReduce/Spark. Map: parse log, emit (error_type, 1). Reduce: count per type. Parallelizes across cluster. Hours instead of days. This is what MapReduce was designed for.
